segments.t: We're still in the nineteen eighties, in the same communal flat. Last time, Vanya's father came home from Hungary with gum, markers and a toy car, and told him to share everything; little Arkady only watched. Now Arkady asks Vanya for a piece of gum, and soon the toy car goes missing. We'll hear it in Russian first; don't worry about catching every word.
Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
Когда вырасту, ты будешь просить у меня прощения!
Let's go through it. The presents have been handed out, and Vanya is enjoying himself in front of Arkady.
'Well, four-eyes?' "Ochkarik" comes from "ochki" ('glasses'), a classic schoolyard taunt for a kid in specs. Then Vanya shows his empty hands.
'See, there's nothing left.' Literally, 'nothing didn't remain': in Russian, "nichego" ('nothing') always pairs with "ne" ('not'). Arkady knows that isn't true.
'But you've still got some.' Literally, 'at you there is more', with tiny "zhe" adding an insistent 'but you clearly do!'. Then he asks.
'Give me just one.' "Day" asks someone casually to hand something over, and "khot odnu" pleads for 'at least one'. The answer is short.
'No. That's mine.' "Moyo" is 'mine' when talking about things in general, even though his father told him to share. Arkady has one word for that.
'Greedy!' "Zhadina" is what Russian kids shout at anyone who won't share. Vanya doesn't care, and shows off his markers.
'See the markers? They're from Japan!' Literally, 'this is Japan' — "eto Yaponiya" — which is how a boy boasts about foreign treasure. Suddenly something goes missing.
А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
'Hey, where's the toy car? Where's my toy car?' "Moya" ends in '-ya' to match "mashinka", since cars are feminine in Russian. Right then Vanya spots Arkady.
'Four-eyes! Grab him!' "Derzhi" is the very same 'hold' Vanya's dad used when handing over gum, except "derzhi yego!" means 'hold him — grab him!'. Arkady struggles.
'Let go!' "Pusti!" is the sharp one-word order to release someone. Vanya grins.
'Well, well, caught you, didn't we?' "Popalsya" packs 'you got caught!' into a single word. Arkady tries to explain.
'I was only looking!' "Tolko" means 'only' or 'just', and "posmotrel" has no '-a' on the end for a male speaker; a girl would say "posmotrela". Vanya gets a nasty idea.
Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
'Look, how dirty our toilet is!' "Smotrite" adds '-te' onto "smotri" because Vanya is calling to all the kids at once. Then he adds something.

'It needs a wash!' "Nado" means 'it's needed' or 'we ought to', and you'll hear it in almost every Russian conversation. What happens next is cruel: the boys dunk Arkady's head into the toilet bowl, and afterwards he makes a threat.
'You'll be sorry!' "Yeshchyo pozhaleyesh" literally warns 'you will still regret it!'. Vanya just laughs at him.
'Oh yeah? When?' "Da nu?" is a scoffing two-word comeback for 'oh really, come off it?'. Arkady answers.
Когда вырасту, ты будешь просить у меня прощения!

'When I grow up, you'll be begging me to forgive you!' Where English uses present in 'when I grow up', Russian uses future "kogda vyrastu" — 'when I will grow up'. Remember this line, because the whole series turns on it.
'What did you say?' "Chto ty skazal?" puts 'what' first and needs no helper like 'did' at all. Here's the whole scene once more.
Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
Когда вырасту, ты будешь просить у меня прощения!
That's the promise little Arkady makes, and thirty years later he will get his chance. See you next time!
